title: Given an array of numbers, find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence, where a subsequence keeps relative order but need not be contiguous. Explain the Longest Common Substring pattern connection, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Longest Increasing Subsequence (Longest Strictly Rising Ordered Subsequence)

s1_definition.profdef: The Longest Increasing Subsequence belongs to the Longest Common Substring family of subsequence dynamic programs. We define, for each index, the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends at that index, built from the best earlier index holding a smaller value. The answer is the maximum over all indices. The simple recurrence is quadratic, and a patience-sorting variant reaches order n log n.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India looks at a customer's monthly closing balances and finds the longest stretch of months, not necessarily consecutive, where the balance kept strictly rising, because a long rising streak signals steady financial health. Rajesh's balances are scanned to find that longest rising subsequence.
s1_definition.oneliner: The best increasing run ending at an index is one plus the best run ending at any earlier smaller value.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Longest Increasing Subsequence belongs to the Longest Common Substring family of subsequence dynamic programs. We define, for each index, the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends at that index, built from the best earlier index holding a smaller value. The answer is the maximum over all indices. The simple recurrence is quadratic, and a patience-sorting variant reaches order n log n.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India looks at a customer's monthly closing balances and finds the longest stretch of months, not necessarily consecutive, where the balance kept strictly rising, because a long rising streak signals steady financial health. Rajesh's balances are scanned to find that longest rising subsequence.

**One line to remember:** The best increasing run ending at an index is one plus the best run ending at any earlier smaller value.

sections.s2_technical:
We define a length array where the entry at index i is the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence that ends with the element at i. Every element alone is a subsequence of length one, so we seed each entry with one. For each i we look back at every earlier index j: if the value at j is strictly less than the value at i, the subsequence ending at j can be extended by the element at i, so the entry at i becomes the larger of itself and one plus the entry at j. The answer is the maximum entry overall, since an increasing subsequence can end anywhere.

Bottom-up: `int[] len = new int[n]; Arrays.fill(len, 1); int best = n == 0 ? 0 : 1; for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) if (a[j] < a[i]) { len[i] = Math.max(len[i], len[j] + 1); best = Math.max(best, len[i]); }`. A concrete check: for balances two, nine, three, six, five, eight, the longest increasing subsequence is two, three, six, eight of length four. Senior nuance: the naive form is quadratic in time, the patience-sorting method with binary search over a tails array is order n log n, and this is a subsequence pattern cousin of longest common subsequence.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India reviews a customer's monthly closing balances and wants the longest stretch of months, not necessarily consecutive, where the balance kept strictly rising, because a long rising streak is a positive signal in a financial health score. Enumerating every subsequence is exponential. This is exactly how the Longest Increasing Subsequence works: it finds that longest rising run with the best-earlier-smaller recurrence.

The code defines a `BalanceTrendService` exposing `longestRisingStreak(balances)` returning the length of the longest increasing subsequence. A `Demo` runs it over a sample balance array and logs the length.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the balance array two, nine, three, six, five, eight. We want the longest strictly rising subsequence.

Step 1 — Every month starts with a best rising run of one, since any single balance is a trivially rising subsequence.

Step 2 — At nine the only earlier smaller value is two, so nine can extend it, giving a run of two ending at nine.

Step 3 — At three the earlier smaller value is two, so three extends it to a run of two. At six the smaller earlier values two and three both work, and extending the run ending at three gives three.

Step 4 — At five the smaller earlier values two and three work, extending the run ending at three to a run of three ending at five. At eight the smaller earlier values include six and five, and extending the run of three ending at six gives four.

Step 5 — The maximum best length is four, the run two, three, six, eight. The answer is four. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:28:03 PM com.bank.trend.service.BalanceTrendService longestRisingStreak
INFO: Longest rising balance streak = 4
Oct 27, 2026 9:28:03 PM com.bank.trend.BalanceTrendApplication main
INFO: Longest strictly rising balance streak length is 4
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: balances = [2, 9, 3, 6, 5, 8]
    │
    ▼
  len[i] = 1 + max(len[j]) over j<i with a[j]<a[i]
    │ 2→1  9→2(after 2)  3→2(after 2)
    │ 6→3(after 2,3)  5→3(after 2,3)  8→4(after 2,3,6)
    ▼
  best = max(len) = 4   (2,3,6,8)
    ▼
  Output: longest rising streak = 4
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Longest Increasing Subsequence is a subsequence dynamic program in the same family as longest common subsequence, and the way I frame it is per ending index. For each index I compute the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence that ends exactly at that element. Every element alone is a subsequence of length one, and to extend I look back at every earlier index holding a strictly smaller value, because the rising run that ends there can be continued by the current element.

So the length ending at an index is one plus the best length ending at any earlier smaller value, and since an increasing subsequence can finish anywhere, the final answer is the maximum length over all indices rather than the last one. The straightforward version is quadratic in time. I always mention the faster patience-sorting approach that keeps a tails array and uses binary search to place each element, which brings it down to order n log n.

At the National Bank of India I used this to examine a customer's monthly closing balances and find the longest stretch of months, not necessarily consecutive, where the balance kept strictly rising, because a long rising streak was a positive signal in a financial health score. I computed the best rising run ending at each month and took the maximum. Explaining the extend-the-best-earlier-smaller recurrence, why the answer is the overall maximum, and the n log n optimisation is what shows an interviewer I understand this member of the subsequence pattern family.
